summary: Specifies the format for DHCPv4 client identifiers so they are interchangeable with the identifiers used in DHCPv6. It also corrects some problems in RFC 2131 and RFC 2132 in how client identifiers are handled. It is standards-track and updates RFC 2131, RFC 2132, and RFC 3315.

plainLanguage.summary: A name tag lets the address-giver recognize the same computer each time. This makes the tag work the same way for old and new versions of the protocol.

subtitle: How a DHCPv4 client names itself with the same stable DUID and IAID that DHCPv6 uses, instead of its network card's address.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 clients were commonly identified by the hardware address of a network interface, so a replaced card, a second interface or a switch between DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 made the same host look like different clients.
tldr.mechanism: Clients put an RFC 3315-style binding identifier in the DHCPv4 client identifier option: type 255, a 32-bit IAID, then a DUID that identifies the host.
tldr.outcome: A host keeps one identity across hardware changes and across DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, while old servers and old clients still interoperate. Later, RFC 5494 updated this document.

today: RFC 4361 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006. It is updated by RFC 5494, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: One Identity for Both DHCP Versions
sections.content:
RFC 4361 says how a DHCPv4 client should identify itself to a server. Conforming clients use a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID), as defined for DHCPv6 in RFC 3315, and carry it in the DHCPv4 client identifier option described in RFC 2132. The behavior here supersedes what RFC 2131 and RFC 2132 specify.

The reason is the move from IPv4 to IPv6. Some devices will use both DHCP versions, and they have a smoother time if they identify themselves the same way in each. The RFC points to DNS updates made by the server on the client's behalf as the most obvious case.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer that talks to two kinds of address-givers should wear the same name tag for both. Then neither one gets confused about who it is.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong With Hardware-Based Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC lists four problems with the older scheme.

  • Identities are ephemeral. RFC 2132 recommends building the client identifier from the permanent link-layer address of the interface. Replace the network hardware and the client loses its IP address and anything tied to the old identifier, such as its published domain name.
  • Accidental multiple identities. A laptop with a wired and a wireless interface looks like two independent hosts. Both present the same name for a directory update but different identities, so only one interface gets the name. Likewise a PXE boot loader and the operating system it loads may present two different identifiers.
  • Incompatible identifiers. RFC 2132 and RFC 3315 derive identifiers differently, so the DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 identifiers are guaranteed to differ.
  • No client identifier required. RFC 2131 lets the server fall back on the client's link-layer address when no identifier is sent, which has the same drawbacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If your name tag is the number on your bike, you become a new person when you get a new bike. And if you own two bikes, people think you are two kids.

sections.title: What a Good Client Identifier Needs
sections.content:
To fix those problems, identifiers must be persistent, so adding or removing hardware does not change them. A client with two interfaces must be able to present two network identities, yet the server must be able to tell they belong to one host. A client may also choose to present exactly the same identifier on two interfaces so that both get the same address. Dual-stack hosts must use the same host identification string for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, for example so that both servers register the same identity in the DNS. Use of the chaddr field as an identifier by DHCPv4 clients must be deprecated.

Compatibility is also required: non-conforming servers must handle identifiers from conforming clients, and conforming servers must work with non-conforming clients.

The answer needs two parts: one unique to the host and one unique to the network identity being presented. The DUID and the Identity Association Identifier (IAID) from RFC 3315 fit, and the RFC concludes they are the only possible solution.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag needs a part for who you are and a part for which door you are using. That way you stay one person, but people can still tell your doors apart.

sections.title: The Client Identifier Option Layout
sections.content:
The general format of the option comes from section 9.14 of RFC 2132. To carry an RFC 3315-style binding identifier, the type byte of the client identifier option is set to 255. The type is followed by the IAID, an opaque 32-bit quantity, and the DUID takes all the remaining contents of the option. The option code is 61 and the length byte is n.

RFC 2132 section 9.14 is rewritten to match: the client identifier consists of a type field whose value is normally 255, a four-byte IA_ID field, then the client's DUID from RFC 3315 section 9. The text saying the minimum length is 2 is deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag has a label saying what kind of tag it is, then a number for which door, then the long name of the computer.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Behave
sections.content:
A conforming DHCPv4 client MUST use stable node identifiers and MUST NOT use identifiers based solely on a hard-wired layer-two address, such as an Ethernet MAC address, except as allowed in section 9.2 of RFC 3315. It MUST send a client identifier containing an IAID and a DUID. A client that generates a DUID and has stable storage MUST keep it, even across an operating system reboot.

DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 clients SHOULD let an operator learn and configure the DUID. A device configured by both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 SHOULD use the same DUID for both without operator help. A client with several interfaces SHOULD use the same DUID on every interface and a different IAID on each.

No change is required of servers that already follow RFC 2131 and RFC 2132. Conforming servers MUST use the client identifier option to identify the client when it is sent. A server MAY use administrator-supplied chaddr and htype values to identify a client when the administrator is assigning it a fixed IP address, even if the client sends an identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer should keep the same name tag forever, even after it is switched off, and wear it on every door. The address-giver should read the tag when there is one.

sections.title: Edits to RFC 2131 and RFC 2132
sections.content:
The RFC spells out wording changes so the older documents do not contradict it. In RFC 2131 it removes the example that a client identifier may hold a hardware address identical to chaddr. The sentence saying a client MAY provide an identifier becomes: the client MUST explicitly provide one and MUST use the same option in all messages. The advice about using chaddr, serial numbers or DNS names is replaced by: the client MUST NOT rely on chaddr to identify it. A client MAY include a different unique identifier becomes MUST include a unique identifier, and the places where chaddr could stand in for the client identifier are deleted.

These changes do not stop a server from using chaddr when a client sends no identifier. Servers MUST still do that to support old clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook said a name tag was optional. The new pages say every computer must wear one, but the address-giver still helps computers that forgot theirs.

sections.title: Multi-Stage Network Booting
sections.content:
A single device may run several DHCP clients in sequence, such as a network boot loader and then the operating system. If each uses a different identifier, or the first uses none, the server allocates a different IP address to each stage. Some servers work around the common case where the boot PROM sends no identifier and the operating system sends one built from the MAC address, by treating them as the same. A compliant client does not build identifiers from the MAC address, so that trick stops working, which the RFC says may have significant impact at some sites.

The RFC gives suggestions rather than requirements. Boot loader clients should ask for short lease times and send a DHCPRELEASE before moving on. The final-stage client should, where possible, set the boot PROM's DUID to match the operating system's. Clients used only for multi-stage booting, never expected to boot over DHCPv6, with a MAC address that cannot be easily changed, may not need these changes, though the RFC says the first suggestion is definitely better.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer starts up in steps, each step may introduce itself differently and get its own address. The advice is to give back the address between steps and to use the same name tag throughout.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no new security issues. It points to section 7 of RFC 2131 and to RFC 3118 (authentication for DHCP messages) for DHCPv4 exposure, and to section 23 of RFC 3315 for DHCPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the name tag does not make anything riskier. The existing safety advice still applies.
